blocks.text: Tying finches together, he sells seven for one obol. For an obol, that is, for two assaria, or asses. This is shown by these words of Polybius, Histories book 2: Ὡς μὲν οὖν ἐπιτοπολὺ παρίενται τοὺς καταλύτας οἱ πανδοχεῖς ἡμιασσαρίου, τοῦτο δ᾽ ἐστὶ τέταρτον μέρος ὀβολοῦ [Hōs men oun epitopoly pariентai tous katalytas hoi pandocheis hēmiassariou, touto d᾽ esti tetarton meros obolou]. Innkeepers generally receive their guests for half an as, or half an assarion, which is a quarter of an obol. So when Christ says that five sparrows are sold for two [II, 737] assaria, it is the same as if he had said they are sold for an obol. From this you may infer that at Athens in the time of Aristophanes provisions were somewhat cheaper than in Judaea in the time of Christ. For at the price for which the Athenians bought seven finches, the Jews bought only five sparrows. Further, the Latin translator of Aristophanes has passeres [sparrows] for fringilli [finches], because the sparrow and the finch are very similar birds. Hence the Glosses [col. 159] of Philoxenus: Σπίνος· ὁ στρουθὸς [Spinos; ho strouthos], Frincillus, fringillus, as if σπίνος [spinos] were the same as στρουθὸς [strouthos], or passer [sparrow]. Fringillus is in French pinson, formerly perhaps pintion, like σπίνθιον [spinthion] in Hesychius. So too chanson from cantione, maison from mansione, raison from ratione, etc. But whether five or seven such little birds are sold for an obol, and whether the author of the Mishnah valued the mother alone, or the mother with her young, at an as, they must be very cheap animals, since they are on sale for so slight a price. Yet here Christ teaches us that even these little creatures are such a concern to God that none of them falls to the ground without him, that is, perishes without his permission. With this agrees Luke: Ἓν ἐξ αὐτῶν οὐκ ἔστιν ἐπιλελησμένον ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ [Hen ex autōn ouk estin epilelēsmenon enōpion tou Theou]; Not one of them is forgotten before God. The phrase is taken from Psal. IX, 19., where it is said of the poor man: Οὐκ εἰς τέλος ἐπιλησθήσεται [Ouk eis telos epilēsthēsetai], He shall not be forgotten for ever; in Hebrew לא לנצח ישכח. Hence the royal Psalmist, of small and great animals alike, Psal. CIV, 27.: These all wait upon you, that you may give them their food in due season. Yet, to say nothing for the present of the Jews, most of whom hold a different opinion, Jerome on Habakkuk ch. 1 says this: It is absurd to lower the majesty of God to this, that he should know at every moment how many gnats are born and how many die; how great is the multitude of bugs, fleas and flies on the earth; how many fish swim in the water; and which of the smaller must fall prey to the larger. Let us not be such foolish flatterers of God that, while we drag his power down to the lowest things, we do injury to ourselves, saying that the providence over rational and irrational creatures is the same. These words might seem rather harsh unless softened by a kindly interpretation, so that we understand them to be said comparatively (as he hints toward the end): lest God be thought to have the same regard for brutes as for men, whom he created in his own image, since he preserves the brutes chiefly for the sake of men, for whose use they were created. We therefore recognize different degrees of divine providence, and that God does not care for oxen in the same way as for men, as Paul teaches, 1 Cor. IX, 9. Yet it is certain that oxen as well as men, and even the meanest [col. 160] creatures, are subject to God. Nor does he disdain to govern and preserve what he deigned to create. And we must beware of inventing limits to that providence, which, as the greatest things do not burden it, so the smallest do not escape it or go neglected by it. Who would believe that God did not know the number of the quails with which he fed the Israelites in the desert, or of the fish that swam in the lake of Gennesaret when Peter cast his nets at Christ's command? Or that he did not know how many frogs or lice he would use against the Egyptians; or that those locusts which are called God's army, Ioel. II, 11., were of no [II, 738] concern to him, and that this supreme commander did not know how many soldiers he had enlisted in his army? Finally, what could be plainer than Christ's words, that none of the sparrows falls to the ground without God, or is forgotten before him? On this passage note what the most learned Buxtorf cites from the Jerusalem Talmud in his Lexicon Talmudicum, p. 553: Rabbi Simeon ben Yochai was hiding in a cave. One day, sitting at the mouth of the cave and seeing a fowler catching birds and spreading his net, he heard a daughter of the voice (an oracle); when it said דימוס dimos (that is, release), the bird escaped. But when the daughter of the voice said ספיקולא, spicula (that is, sentence of death), the bird was caught. Then the oracle said, צפור מבלברי שמיא לא יבדא כל שכן בר נשא, A little bird does not perish without heaven (that is, without God's will and providence): how much less a man! For לא יבדא read לא יאבד. The pagans too write things not unlike these. Thus Plutarch somewhere proves from Homer that the ancients held the opinion that by the divine power are cared for οὐ μόνον βόας, ἀλλὰ καὶ πάντα τὰ ἄλλα ζῶα [ou monon boas, alla kai panta ta alla zōa], not only oxen, but all other animals too. And Aelian, Hist. book 11, ch. 31: Ἴδιον δὲ ἄρα τῶν ζώων καὶ ἐκεῖνο ἀγαθὸν, πρόνοιαν αὐτῶν καὶ οἱ Θεοὶ ποιοῦνται, καὶ οὔτε αὐτῶν καταφρονοῦσιν, οὐδὲ μὴν ὀλιγώρως ἔχουσιν [Idion de ara tōn zōōn kai ekeino agathon, pronoian autōn kai hoi Theoi poiountai, kai oute autōn kataphronousin, oude mēn oligōrōs echousin]; The brutes too have this good, that the gods provide for them, and neither despise them nor treat them with indifference.
